data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The dominant cross-city modulator of nocturnal UHI is sky view factor: dense urban street canyons with tall buildings restrict the view of the cold sky, reducing the rate at which urban surfaces lose heat by longwave radiative exchange. After sunset, both city and country cool by longwave radiation, but urban surfaces in deep canyons see only a narrow patch of sky and exchange infrared radiation partly with warm building walls rather than the cold sky dome, dramatically slowing their cooling. The single best cross-city modulator is building height and street geometry: cities with taller buildings, narrower streets, and lower sky view factors cool more slowly at night, producing a larger nocturnal temperature gap.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If nocturnal UHI were strongest in low-density suburban cities with high sky view factor, the SVF mechanism would be contradicted.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the gap did not increase with building height or density but instead tracked anthropogenic emissions or vegetation, SVF would lose explanatory primacy.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If removing canyon geometry effects statistically still left the bulk of the nocturnal gap unexplained, SVF alone would be insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Nocturnal cooling is governed by net longwave radiation: a surface cools by emitting infrared to the sky and warms by absorbing infrared from its surroundings. In open countryside, surfaces see nearly the full cold sky and cool rapidly. In a street canyon, the sky view factor is reduced; surfaces exchange radiation with each other (warm walls, warm ground) in a partial radiative trap, and the effective cold-sink is the small visible sky patch. This radiative coupling among warm surfaces slows cooling citywide. The effect scales with canyon geometry: deeper, denser canyons (lower SVF) trap more radiation and cool more slowly, so cities with greater building height and built density have larger nocturnal UHI.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
